strengths: Datasets/Benchmarks contribution is well motivated and fills a clear gap: existing EO benchmarks (Tab. 1) have few modalities, are mostly regional, and lack explicitly held-out geographic splits. MMEarth-Bench provides five novel global tasks (biomass, three soil properties, species occurrence), 12 aligned modalities, random and geographic (Africa) test splits, and 5%/50%/100% low-shot training subsets, all sharing the same modality suite as the MMEarth pretraining corpus.

The benchmarking study is unusually thorough: 7 recent pretrained models spanning RGB-only, S2-only, and multimodal architectures (including DINOv3 Web/Sat, TerraMind, Copernicus-FM), full finetuning plus linear probing, three seeds with standard errors, Wilcoxon significance tests, per-model rank analyses, and complete raw results in the supplementary.

The empirical findings are informative for the community: (multimodal) pretraining helps in low-shot settings, but all models show substantial geographic generalization gaps on 4/5 tasks; multimodal finetuning can even harm out-of-region generalization (Fig. 6), which the authors connect to prior work on fusion-module overfitting.

TTT-MMR is a sensible, model-agnostic method: using auxiliary modalities as reconstruction targets at test time sidesteps the modality-compatibility constraint of existing pretrained models, and gradient normalization across modalities plus geographic batching (TTT-MMR-GEO) is a reasonable approach to TTT regularization. Improvements over joint training are consistent across all 8 models, 5 tasks, and both splits, with statistical support.

Reproducibility artifacts are strong: detailed dataset-generation pipeline (sensor filtering, cloud masking, tile construction, per-modality no-data handling) in the supplementary, H5 formats with documentation, a map-based data explorer, a practitioner's guide for extracting modalities for new tasks, inference cost measurements (<1 s/sample), and a link to code/data.
weaknesses: The geographic test split conflates geographic shift with strong label distribution shift (Tab. S.4: e.g., biomass mean 26 vs 65 Mg/ha, soil OC mean 25 vs 81 g/kg in Africa vs training regions). Since R2 is computed against the geographic test labels, the reported 'geographic generalization gap' partially reflects label shift that no source-only model could fully close; a more careful decomposition or discussion of this confound is needed.

The species task labels are derived from IUCN range polygons rather than observations, so presence/absence is largely a smooth spatial quantity. With geolocation (and biome/ecoregion) included as input modalities, mAP approaching 0.99 (Copernicus-FM, Tab. S.15) raises a shortcut/leakage concern that the paper does not analyze; conclusions about representation quality on this task may be inflated.

Absolute gains from TTT-MMR are modest and somewhat fragile: raw tables (e.g., Tabs. S.16-S.30) show small deltas, occasional degradation relative to plain finetuning (FT), and geographic-split R2 for soil N/OC that is mostly negative before and after TTT. The per-sample adaptation cost (up to ~0.9 s vs 0.007 s forward pass) is non-trivial relative to the gains.

The method evaluation lacks comparisons against other plausible TTA baselines adapted to regression (e.g., self-supervised rotation prediction at test time, pseudo-label self-training, or regularization variants), so it is hard to attribute the improvement specifically to multimodal reconstruction versus generic test-time training with any auxiliary signal. Ablations of the design choices (gradient normalization, number of modalities, I_max, batch size) are also limited.

Benchmark fairness concerns: models range from an attosized MPMAE (trained on 56x56 images) to ViT-L models, yet a single shared finetuning recipe is applied to all; the finding that the tiny MPMAE is competitive suggests tuning or capacity effects that are not disentangled. The Copernicus-FM multimodal evaluation requires a newly designed Siamese finetuning setup, which introduces investigator-design choices into the ranking.

Missing modality handling is uneven across modalities (e.g., Sentinel-1 has ~60% NaN tiles for some tasks per Tab. S.3), and the paper does not analyze how pervasive missing modalities affect TTT-MMR's adaptation signal, which is central to the method.

Accessibility/reproducibility is partly unverified in the manuscript: project page, code, and explorer URLs are blank in the text, and data is hosted on a university server; long-term availability and licensing of the species task ('Terms of Use') may constrain redistribution.

strengths: Contribution type: although no type is declared, this is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution (with an accompanying method); under that framing the evidence is generally appropriate — the primary value lies in the benchmark, and the method should not be required to be a major algorithmic advance.

MMEarth-Bench is a genuinely useful addition: five global tasks (biomass, three soil properties, species occurrence) with 12 aligned modalities shared across tasks, random and geographic (held-out Africa) test splits, and 5%/50%/100% low-shot subsets directly targeting the three identified grand challenges (label sparsity, geographic shift, modality ambiguity).

The comparison to existing benchmarks (Tab. 1) is well argued: prior EO benchmarks rarely combine global coverage, explicit whole-region held-out splits, and more than 3 modalities per task, so the gap being filled is real.

The benchmarking study is broad and careful: 7 pretrained models spanning RGB-only, S2-only, and multimodal architectures, plus a random-init control, finetuning and linear probing, three seeds, raw per-seed numbers in the supplement, Wilcoxon tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction, and informative negative findings (multimodal inputs can hurt geographic generalization; DINOv3 Sat pretraining adds little).

TTT-MMR is model-agnostic and simple; the use of all test-time modalities as reconstruction targets (rather than inputs) is a reasonable way to exploit modality mismatch, and geographic batching is an interesting regularization/specialization trade-off; the <1 sec/sample inference cost is a practical plus.

The supplementary is unusually thorough: dataset construction details, missing-modality statistics, raw result tables for every seed and split, a practitioner's guide, and an interactive explorer, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The absolute magnitude of the TTT-MMR gains is small for many models/tasks (Figs. 7 and S.15 show median improvements often below 0.05 R2; relative improvements under ~10% for most models), and gains shrink for the multimodal models that are the paper's main motivating class; the claim that this 'boosts model performance' across the board is technically supported but the practical significance is modest.

The geographic evaluation rests on a single held-out region (Africa). One shift domain cannot establish general geographic generalization ability or characterize TTT-MMR-Geo behavior across domain types; a second held-out region would substantially strengthen the core claims.

The species task is built from IUCN range polygons, i.e., coarse expert-drawn presence envelopes sampled by bounding-box rejection, not occurrence data; tiles far outside a plausible habitat can be labeled as a species' presence. This pseudo-label structure plus heavy spatial autocorrelation makes the 'clearest and most consistent model rankings' on species hard to interpret as real occurrence prediction, and the task may reward memorizing coarse range geometry (mAP ~0.99 for Copernicus-FM suggests near-trivial separability in-distribution).

Biomass labels are GEDI L4A footprint-level model estimates rather than direct measurements, and the paper does not discuss how label noise/model bias (e.g., saturation, biome-dependent errors) interacts with the reported R2 and geographic gaps; a more careful treatment of label provenance for at least two of the five tasks is needed.

Some design choices are under-justified: TTT hyperparameters (|B|=8, lambda=1e-2, Imax=5) and the decision to reset the encoder after each batch are stated rather than analyzed; the number of TTT iterations is tuned on validation batches, but sensitivity and failure modes of TTT (negative deltas appear in Fig. 7) are not characterized.

The method contribution is incremental relative to prior TTT/joint-training work: it is essentially JT's auxiliary reconstruction losses reused as the TTA signal with per-modality gradient normalization and a geographic batching heuristic; no comparison against alternative TTA baselines (e.g., TENT variants adapted to regression, S4T-style synchronization) is provided on the benchmark.

Nomenclature is confusing: the benchmark shares its name with the existing MMEarth pretraining dataset [42] (a benchmarked model, MPMAE, is pretrained on it), which will complicate citation and searchability.

Several multimodal/soil-task results on the geographic split are at or below zero R2 (Tabs. S12, S13), meaning models are worse than predicting the mean; the paper reports this but does not sufficiently discuss what this implies about the difficulty or label quality of these tasks, or about how meaningful averaged rankings (Tab. 5) are when most per-task values are degenerate.

strengths: Genuinely novel benchmark contribution: MMEarth-Bench provides five new environmental tasks (biomass, three soil properties, species occurrence) with 12 consistently aligned modalities, global coverage, and — importantly — both random and geographic (Africa held-out) test splits, addressing concrete gaps in existing EO benchmarks (Tab. 1 shows the comparison convincingly).

The dataset construction is unusually thorough and transparent: tile generation procedures, quality filters, split statistics, missing-modality analysis, and label distributions are all documented in the supplementary, and a visualization explorer plus code for extracting the 12 modalities for new (lon, lat) locations greatly enhance reproducibility and practical utility.

Benchmarking of 7 recent pretrained models (RGB-only, S2-only, multimodal) yields several scientifically interesting findings: multimodal pretraining helps in low-shot settings, but geographic generalization remains poor for all models (substantial drops on 4/5 tasks), and multimodal *finetuning* can sometimes hurt geographic generalization — a nuanced and practically relevant insight.

TTT-MMR is a sensible, model-agnostic use of test-time modalities as reconstruction targets (rather than inputs), distinguishing itself from prior multimodal TTA (READ, MM-TTA) and from joint training; per-modality gradient normalization is a reasonable design choice, and improvements over the JT baseline are statistically validated (Wilcoxon with Holm-Bonferroni correction) across models, tasks, and both splits.

The batching study (random vs. geographic batching) directly addresses the regularization/specialization trade-off known to be crucial in TTT, and the practitioner's guide with per-sample inference times supports usability.
Evidence is broad: 3 seeds, 3 training-data regimes (5/50/100%), finetuning and linear probing, raw per-seed numbers provided in the supplementary.
weaknesses: The practical magnitude of the TTT gains is modest: relative improvements are often only a few percent (e.g., ~0.4-9% RI, and Copernicus-FM gains under 1%), while the geographic generalization gap the paper motivates remains largely unclosed (soil OC on the geographic split is near or below zero R² even after TTT). The method helps, but the headline challenge is far from solved, which slightly tempers the methodological contribution.

There is a clear risk of benchmark design favoring certain models: all tasks reuse exactly the MMEarth pretraining modalities, so models whose pretraining matches the benchmark (e.g., MPMAE) have a structural advantage, and this circularity (same group, same modalities) is not critically discussed as a limitation.

The species task uses IUCN range-map polygons as labels, which are model-derived presence/absence products rather than observations; the near-perfect mAP (0.99) of Copernicus-FM on the random split suggests the task may be largely solvable from landcover/geolocation cues, raising questions about its discriminative power as a benchmark.

Only Africa serves as the geographic test region; a single held-out continent limits the generality of the geographic-generalization conclusions, and the Africa polygon is manually drawn in QGIS, which should be better specified for reproducibility.

Some experimental details invite scrutiny: Imax for TTT is selected using validation batches per-model, which is reasonable but means compute cost of TTT is partly hidden; heterogeneous model scales (an attosized MPMAE vs. ViT-L models) complicate the cross-model ranking interpretation; the finetuning protocol (full finetuning of all parameters with a single hyperparameter configuration) may disadvantage larger models.

The formalization contains a technically sloppy chain rule (∂Rm/∂θ = ∂Rm/∂hα ∂hα/∂eθ ∂eθ/∂θ, treating the frozen decoder parameter α as a differentiable node), which does not affect the method but indicates imprecise writing; minor typos elsewhere (e.g., 'continuos-valued').

The main text lacks an explicit limitations section; weaknesses such as soil-task label aggregation, missing-modality rates (Sentinel-1 NaN rates of ~57-62% are significant and under-analyzed in the main paper), and the narrowness of the geographic split deserve prominent treatment.

strengths: MMEarth-Bench addresses a real gap: existing EO benchmarks offer few modalities per task, limited global distribution, and rarely explicit geographic test splits. The paper's five tasks with 12 shared modalities, globally distributed tiles, and both random and geographic (Africa) test splits constitute a valuable, reusable community resource (Datasets/Benchmarks contribution), complemented by an interactive Explorer tool and detailed generation pipeline.

The benchmarking is unusually thorough: 8 recent pretrained models (RGB, S2-only, multimodal) across 3 training-data regimes, both splits, 3 seeds, finetuning and linear probing, with rankings, significance tests (Wilcoxon with Holm-Bonferroni), and complete raw results in the appendix. The honest findings (randomly initialized multimodal model competitive; all models fail geographic generalization on 4/5 tasks) are informative for the community and counter prevailing optimism about foundation-model generalization.

TTT-MMR is a clean, model-agnostic formulation: joint training with a lightweight modality reconstruction decoder, per-modality gradient normalization, frozen decoder at test time. Geographic batching (TTT-MMR-Geo) is a sensible regularization/specialization trade-off, and the long-tail analysis (Fig. 8) provides a mechanistic explanation of when it helps. Gains are demonstrated across all models, tasks, and splits with statistical support, and a practitioner's guide plus compute-time analysis (<1 s/sample) establish practical usability.

Reproducibility is strong: exhaustive dataset documentation (per-modality missingness, statistics, H5/TIFF formats, sampling code), hyperparameter tables, code/data hosting commitments, and near-complete raw numbers in the appendix.
weaknesses: Label quality is a concern for the regression tasks. Biomass comes from GEDI's model-derived AGBD product (not direct measurements), and soil properties are sparse WoSIS point measurements aggregated per tile; the paper does not quantify how label noise might interact with the reported R^2 ceilings and the geographic generalization gap (e.g., Africa's lower label density in WoSIS is both the motivation for the split and a source of distribution mismatch).

Potential proxy leakage between task labels and reconstruction modalities is underexamined: canopy height is explicitly acknowledged to correlate with biomass, and landcover/climate modalities plausibly correlate with soil properties and species ranges. This inflates the intuition that TTT-MMR is a purely self-supervised signal — it functions partly as a label-correlated auxiliary target — and the gains may partly reflect leakage rather than genuine adaptation. The ablations (A.4.5) partially address modality dependence but do not probe this issue directly.

Absolute TTT-MMR gains are small and inconsistent for the strongest models: Table A.17 shows improvements of ~0.0001–0.013 for the best model per task, and Table A.15 shows near-zero or negative relative improvement for Galileo and ConvNeXtV2A-MM on the random split. The method is most useful for weaker/RGB-only models, which slightly tempers the 'improves performance across all models' claim in the abstract (statistically supported, but practically marginal in some regimes).

The geographic generalization evaluation relies on a single held-out region (Africa) per task. While justified for label sparsity, results may not transfer to other types of geographic/domain shift, and the Africa split differs in label distribution as well as geography (Table A.4), conflating covariate and label shift. Additional held-out regions would strengthen the benchmark's generality claims.

Methodological novelty is moderate: TTT with self-supervised auxiliary reconstruction is well established (Sun et al., Gandelsman et al.), and the contribution is the multimodal application, gradient normalization, and geographic batching. This is reasonable for the benchmark context but the method alone would not stand.

Minor presentation issues: the project page URL is missing in the abstract, the Explorer URL is missing in A.1.7, and 'MMEarth-Bench' naming overlaps heavily with the preexisting MMEarth pretraining dataset [42], which could cause confusion; several reconstruction-quality tables (A.19–A.27) are too small to read in the provided form.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: five new globally distributed tasks (biomass, three soil properties, species occurrence) sharing 12 aligned modalities, with both random and geographic (Africa held-out) test splits — this directly addresses gaps in existing EO benchmarks (Tab. 1) regarding modality coverage and global/geographic evaluation.

Extensive and careful benchmarking: 8 recent pretrained models spanning RGB, S2-only, and multimodal architectures, evaluated at 5%/50%/100% training data, on both splits, with linear probing and finetuning, three random seeds, standard errors, and statistical significance testing (one-sided Wilcoxon with Holm-Bonferroni correction).

Honest and informative empirical findings: multimodal pretraining helps in low-shot and geographic-shift regimes, yet a randomly initialized multimodal model is competitive with abundant labels — a useful corrective result for the EO foundation-model community.

The TTT-MMR method is model- and task-agnostic, applied uniformly across 10 models and 5 tasks; geographic batching (TTT-MMR-Geo) is a simple, sensible design, and the long-tail analysis (Fig. 8) shows a concrete, explainable benefit for rare samples.

Exceptional reproducibility artifacts: exhaustive appendix detailing data provenance (GEDI, WoSIS, IUCN), tile generation pipeline, missing-modality statistics, raw per-seed results, a practitioner's guide with compute times, an interactive Explorer tool, and links to dataset/code.

The contribution is best read as Datasets/Benchmarks (plus a feasible method), and judged by that standard the evidence is thorough: dataset design, documentation, and breadth of evaluation are well above typical benchmark-paper standards.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: TTT-MMR is a fairly direct combination of joint training with reconstruction auxiliary tasks (JT/UDA-SS) and test-time training with masked reconstruction (Gandelsman et al.); the per-modality gradient normalization and k-d-tree geographic batching are simple engineering choices rather than conceptual advances.

Absolute and relative gains are modest for strong models: Tab. A.17 shows TTT-MMR-Geo improvements of ~0.001–0.013 for the best per-task models, and Tab. A.15 shows near-zero or negative relative improvement for Copernicus-FM, Galileo, and ConvNeXtV2A-MM on the random split; the headline 'improves performance across all models and tasks' holds only weakly where it matters most (already-strong models).

Label-quality concerns weaken the benchmark's evidential value: biomass labels come from GEDI L4A, which is itself a model-derived estimate, and one of the modalities is the ETH canopy height product trained on related remote-sensing signals — creating potential circularity for the biomass task; similarly, species labels are derived from IUCN range polygons rather than observations, and pretrained models reach ~0.99 mAP on the random split, suggesting the task is largely saturated/trivially predictable from coarse geographic modalities (geolocation, biome, ecoregion).

The geographic generalization evaluation rests on a single held-out region (Africa vs. rest-of-world) per task, limiting the generality of conclusions about geographic robustness; soil labels are also field points aggregated to 1.6 km² tiles, which conflates measurement scale with the model's prediction scale.

The from-scratch multimodal baseline (ConvNeXtV2A-MM) nearly matching or beating all pretrained models on the random split (and often on the geographic split) raises the question of how much the benchmark actually discriminates pretrained-model quality, at least at 100% training data.

Some analysis is under-supported: e.g., the explanation of why multimodal finetuning hurts geographic generalization for TerraMind/Galileo (fusion capacity, domain shift in modalities) is speculative; TTT iteration counts are tuned per batch on validation but then averaged at test time, a somewhat ad hoc protocol.
Reproducibility caveat: data are hosted on a university server with an unspecified availability guarantee, which is a risk for a dataset contribution whose primary value is community reuse.

strengths: MMEarth-Bench fills a genuine gap: no existing EO benchmark combines (i) globally distributed data, (ii) an entire held-out continent (Africa) as a geographic test split, and (iii) many modalities shared across all tasks. The 12 shared modalities across 5 tasks make it uniquely suitable for evaluating multimodal pretrained models, and the comparison table (Tab. 1) situates it well against GEO-Bench, PANGAEA, etc.

The benchmarking study is extensive and honest: 8 pretrained models spanning RGB, S2-only, and multimodal architectures, with 3 seeds, multiple training-data regimes (5/50/100%), finetuning and linear probing, and both test splits. The finding that a randomly initialized multimodal model is competitive with globally pretrained models is a valuable, community-relevant negative result that is well-supported (Tabs. A.10-A.14).

The TTT-MMR method is simple, model-agnostic, and well-motivated: repurposing the multimodal pretext losses as a test-time adaptation signal, with per-modality gradient normalization for stability. Geographic batching (TTT-MMR-Geo) is a sensible regularization/specialization trade-off, and the long-tail analysis (Fig. 8) showing robustness to rare samples is a substantive finding, not just an aggregate average.

Statistical rigor above the norm for benchmark papers: 3 seeds, standard errors, one-sided Wilcoxon tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction, and a clearly defined relative-improvement metric for cross-task aggregation.

Exceptional supplementary material: complete raw results for every experiment, dataset generation details, an interactive Explorer tool, a practitioner's guide (TTT costs <1 s/sample), and per-modality reconstruction analyses and ablations. This strongly supports reproducibility and reuse.

The paper is clearly written, with well-organized related work distinguishing the method from UDA, TENT-style TTA, and multimodal TTA, and it appropriately discusses limitations of existing benchmarks and of the setup itself.
weaknesses: The absolute magnitude of TTT-MMR improvements is modest. For several models (Galileo, ConvNeXtV2A-MM) the RI metric reveals slight degradation on the random split, and per-model gains on some tasks (soil N random split) are on the order of 0.01-0.02 R². The paper acknowledges this but the practical significance for a practitioner could be discussed more directly alongside Tab. A.17.

The geographic shift is confounded with label-distribution shift. The geographic test split (Africa) has very different target distributions (e.g., biomass mean 26.09 vs. 65.14 Mg/ha on random test; Tabs. A.4/A.5), so the observed 'geographic generalization gap' mixes covariate, label, and prior shifts. Only one holdout region (Africa) in one direction is used, limiting conclusions about geographic generalization in general.

Some reconstruction targets appear uninformative in practice: per-modality tables show R² for geolocation encoding as low as -100 to -200 and ecoregion accuracy essentially 0.0000 for many models on the geographic split, suggesting the gradient-normalized aggregation still includes near-useless or badly scaled signals. The method's behavior when such modalities dominate or destabilize the adaptation signal deserves more analysis.

The species task relies on IUCN range polygons, which are expert-drawn coarse polygons rather than occurrence observations; tiles are sampled within bounding boxes and labeled positive if they intersect the range. This introduces label noise and spatial bias, and the multi-label setup (up to 30+ species per tile) means the mAP results are hard to compare to standard species-distribution modeling.

No comparison against alternative TTA baselines beyond JT: TENT is argued to be inapplicable to regression, but the species task is classification, where a TENT comparison would have been natural; other regularization strategies (e.g., entropy-based or batch-norm-style adaptation where applicable, or UDA-SS style methods) are not empirically benchmarked, so the evidence that multimodal reconstruction is the best adaptation signal for this setting is indirect.

Hyperparameter sensitivity of the TTT procedure is underexplored: only |B|=8, λ=1e-2, I_max=5 are used, with I_max tuned on validation. Given the paper's own emphasis on the delicate specialization/regularization trade-off in TTT, an ablation over these would strengthen the method claims.

The benchmark restricts itself to the natural-world domain (biomass, soil, species), and modalities include derived map products (ETH Canopy Height, Dynamic World, ESA WorldCover) that are themselves ML outputs correlated with the labels (canopy height is a strong biomass proxy). This is legitimate for the TTT setting but blurs the line between 'sensor modality' and label proxy, and is worth flagging for future users.

Reproducibility caveats: data is hosted on a university server and much of the pipeline depends on Google Earth Engine, whose results can drift over time (cloud filters, 2020 imagery); no pinned dataset DOI is evident in the main text (the project-page link is empty in the reviewed version).
